opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's not that I think pretraining is unimportant. It's probably the most important part of the whole pipeline. My hesitation is more about whether it's a good place for an individual researcher, especially a student or someone early in their career, to build a research identity.

The first issue is resources. Meaningful pretraining research needs a lot of compute. Many effects only show up at scale. Something that looks great at a hundred million parameters can vanish or even reverse at tens of billions. If you're in academia or a small lab, you're often studying a regime that the frontier has already left behind. You can do careful work and still not know whether your conclusions transfer.

The second issue is the feedback loop. In post-training or evaluation work, you can try an idea and see a result in days. In pretraining, one run can take weeks, and you usually can't afford many seeds or ablations. So you learn slowly, and the signal is noisy. For someone still building research taste, that's a hard environment. You don't get many repetitions.

The third issue is credit and visibility. A lot of real pretraining progress happens inside big companies, and it comes from engineering and data work: data mixtures, filtering, deduplication, infrastructure stability. That work is enormously valuable, but it's often not published, and when it is, it's spread across a big team. It's hard to point to and say, "This was my contribution." If you need a clear research narrative for a PhD or a job market, that's a real cost.

And finally, a lot of the low-hanging fruit at small scale has been picked. The questions that remain tend to be either very expensive to answer or very empirical, more like "this recipe works better for this model at this time" than a lasting insight.

So when someone asks me, I don't say "don't do it." I ask whether they have access to serious compute and a team that's actually training models. If they do, it can be incredibly rewarding, because you're shaping the foundation everything else depends on. If they don't, I usually suggest finding a question where they can move fast, own the result, and still learn something about how these models work. You can always come back to pretraining once you're in an environment that supports it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's because pretraining is a very unforgiving kind of research, and I don't want to romanticize it for someone who hasn't lived through it.

First, the feedback loop is brutally slow. In most areas of machine learning you can run an experiment in an afternoon and know whether your idea works. In pretraining, a single meaningful run can take days or weeks, and it costs a lot of money. So you might get only a handful of real "shots" in a year. If you make a mistake in the data pipeline or a learning rate schedule, you often don't find out until the run is half over. That kind of latency does something to you psychologically. You can't iterate your way to intuition the way you would elsewhere; you have to be right more often than you're wrong, with far fewer chances to practice.

Second, the work is extremely dependent on resources you don't control. Whether you can do good pretraining research is decided largely by how much compute and how much clean data your organization gives you, not by how clever you are. I've seen very talented people spend years without enough compute to test their ideas properly, and it's demoralizing. If you're a student or at a small lab, you may end up doing what I'd call "pretraining-adjacent" work, scaling laws on tiny models, ablations that may not transfer, and you never really know whether your conclusions hold at the scale that matters.

Third, a lot of the job is not glamorous. People imagine architecture breakthroughs, but most of the time you're debugging data deduplication, chasing a loss spike, fixing a tokenizer edge case, or trying to understand why the eval went down by half a point. It's closer to engineering and operations than to the kind of science people picture. Some people love that, and those people thrive. But if you came in wanting to publish elegant ideas, you can be very unhappy.

And finally, there's a credit problem. Pretraining is deeply collaborative, and the output is usually one big model with dozens or hundreds of names behind it. It's hard to point to a result and say, "that was me." For a career, especially an academic one, that's a real cost.

So when someone asks me, I don't say no. I say: be honest with yourself about whether you'll have the compute, whether you can tolerate slow feedback, and whether you're motivated by the craft itself rather than by recognition. If the answer to all three is yes, it's one of the most important things you can work on. If not, there are many areas where you'll learn faster and be happier.

astra-6.text:
I hesitate because pretraining research can require a huge investment before you get clear feedback. You might have an interesting idea, but testing it properly depends on compute, data, and an engineering setup that lets you trust the results. If an experiment doesn’t work, it can be difficult to tell whether the idea was wrong or something else in the pipeline went wrong.

So I’d distinguish between saying the research is important and saying it’s a good choice for a particular person. With the right resources and collaborators, it can be very rewarding. Without that support, you can spend a lot of time getting experiments to run and still have little evidence about the question you wanted to answer. That’s why I’d be cautious about recommending it broadly.

sol-6.1.text:
I hesitate because pretraining research has a very high barrier to entry. You need compute, data, and a reliable engineering setup before you can really test an idea. And the feedback cycle can be long: if a run doesn’t work, it may be hard to tell whether the idea was wrong or something went wrong in the implementation.

That doesn’t mean it isn’t worth doing. But there’s a difference between finding a field exciting and recommending that someone commit years to it. I’d want to understand what resources they have, who they can work with, and whether they enjoy that kind of slow, uncertain experimentation.
